extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10. In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10. Copyright © 2026 Airways Publishing LLC. All rights reserved. ‍

coreStoryFacts.text: The head of the Federal Aviation Administration said a software problem will delay its certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10 as the agency assesses whether it poses a safety issue, a potential setback for the manufacturer as it seeks to complete government approval of its best-selling family of aircraft.
Boeing had expected to receive a green light from its regulator on the years-delayed planes "very soon," CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month.
"We continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process," Boeing said in a statement.
The company had originally planned to start delivering the Max 10 in 2020 before those safety concerns and other problems delayed the plane.
It is the last of the Max family waiting to be certified.
A flight control system was implicated in those crashes.

"We haven't concluded whether this is a safety-of-flight issue or not, but we will be delaying the 10 ... until we're satisfied that we don't have an issue here," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference on air traffic modernization in Washington, D.C., on Monday.
Boeing shares extended earlier losses after Bedford's comments, shedding nearly 7% Monday, as investors assessed another delay after years of setbacks for the aircraft.
It isn't clear how that could affect deliveries of those planes to customers like Southwest Airlines .

Boeing said over the weekend that the issue could occur with a vertical navigation system after an aircraft misses an approach and has to go around and line up to land again, such as in situations when there is an obstruction on the runway, for example.
Both the company and Bedford said pilots are trained for those circumstances.
Bedford said Boeing had fixed a previous bug in the system but "unexpectedly ... introduced a new bug."
The impending certification of the long-awaited Boeing 737 MAX 10 could be delayed, following the assessment that a potential software problem has come to light.
The Federal Aviation Administration ( FAA ) is currently assessing whether this poses a wider safety issue, which means another setback for the American plane maker.

passages: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft.
Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10.
Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported.

In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem.
The FAA's statement did not address either program.
Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps."

Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review.

Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September .
Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more .
In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year.
He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months."
CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward.
The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers.
CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment.
Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes."

In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week .
Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10. In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10. Copyright © 2026 Airways Publishing LLC. All rights reserved. ‍

passages: Cloudflare recently announced early access to Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation , a service that uses frontier models to identify application-specific vulnerabilities and deploy WAF mitigations to block targeted exploits while engineers fix the code.
Cloudflare connects source-code findings to production traffic and security signals.
We can identify whether the affected route is active, and how much traffic it receives.
Cloudflare’s combination of reverse proxy and forward proxy services makes this correlation especially powerful.
Application Security signals can reveal attempts to exploit a public-facing application, while Cloudflare One can surface subsequent activity across corporate traffic.

Connecting these datasets can link an external attack with unusual access, internal scanning, or potential lateral movement, turning separate alerts into a timeline of compromise and helping analysts intervene before the breach progresses.

We address this challenge by connecting application security across four activities that are too often separated: discovering which risks matter, governing what humans and agents may do, protecting applications at runtime, and turning every investigation into stronger protection.
Cloudflare can deliver this framework because of its broad security portfolio and visibility across a vast share of Internet traffic.
Alongside the framework, we connect existing Cloudflare solutions with new capabilities across each stage.

These include: using Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct a penetration test of our Web Application Firewall (WAF), expanding threat intelligence to all customers, and a new feature to automate deploying positive security.

More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, which gives us visibility into attack infrastructure, payload mutations, emerging techniques, and coordinated campaigns at a scale that few organizations can match.
Patterns that look isolated from the perspective of one application can become clear across our network.
This combination of global threat intelligence, local application context, and inline enforcement powers every stage of the framework.
That local context includes which code is deployed, which endpoints are exposed, what legitimate traffic looks like, which identities are acting, and which controls are already active.
Because Cloudflare is inline, we can turn those insights into protections immediately.
A vulnerability buried deep inside your code is harder to exploit if it can’t be reached from the outside.
Our Security Analyst team has already used LLM-based red teaming to test customer applications and our own runtime detections, turning the findings into improved detections for all customers.

We are now developing Adaptive Security, a self-service capability that will periodically pentest selected URLs behind Cloudflare, using LLM-powered agents to identify vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable before attackers find them.
In the AI era, a new layered approach is emerging to best filter traffic from malicious requests:
Cloudflare is the adaptive security control plane for applications, APIs, and agents.
Cloudflare is building a platform to automate security operations.
Deterministic workflows establish the customer and investigation context using trigger history, traffic baselines, enforcement outcomes, and network observations.

sources.title: Cloudflare launches ‘Adaptive Intelligence’ to fight AI-era bot attacks in real time
passages: Cloudflare has announced Adaptive Intelligence, a new continuous detection engine built into its Bot Management platform that is designed to detect and respond to automated cyberattacks in real time.The company said the technology uses insights from trillions of requests across Cloudflare’s global network to continuously learn from live internet traffic and automatically generate short-lived rules aimed at blocking emerging bot attacks.The move comes as automated cyberattacks become easier and cheaper to launch.

Cloudflare said modern AI tools, compromised-device networks and software that can mimic human behaviour have lowered the technical and financial barriers for attackers.Also Read: AI cyber risk is biggest immediate threat to global financial stability: FSB chair Andrew BaileyFor online businesses, this creates an uneven playing field: attackers can make repeated, low-cost attempts, while security teams need to identify and stop threats immediately without blocking legitimate users.Cloudflare says traditional security tools are too slowAccording to Cloudflare, many conventional security systems continue to depend on fixed rules and scheduled updates, which can take weeks or months to deploy.

Cloudflare said it can analyse behavioural patterns across multiple timeframes to identify threats such as slow credential-stuffing and scraping campaigns, which can evade traditional detection systems.Another component of the system combines browser-level session behaviour signals from Cloudflare Precursor with telemetry from Cloudflare's global network.

coreStoryFacts.text: Cloudflare recently announced early access to Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation , a service that uses frontier models to identify application-specific vulnerabilities and deploy WAF mitigations to block targeted exploits while engineers fix the code.
Cloudflare connects source-code findings to production traffic and security signals.
We can identify whether the affected route is active, and how much traffic it receives.
Cloudflare’s combination of reverse proxy and forward proxy services makes this correlation especially powerful.
Application Security signals can reveal attempts to exploit a public-facing application, while Cloudflare One can surface subsequent activity across corporate traffic.

Connecting these datasets can link an external attack with unusual access, internal scanning, or potential lateral movement, turning separate alerts into a timeline of compromise and helping analysts intervene before the breach progresses.

We address this challenge by connecting application security across four activities that are too often separated: discovering which risks matter, governing what humans and agents may do, protecting applications at runtime, and turning every investigation into stronger protection.
Cloudflare can deliver this framework because of its broad security portfolio and visibility across a vast share of Internet traffic.
Alongside the framework, we connect existing Cloudflare solutions with new capabilities across each stage.

These include: using Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct a penetration test of our Web Application Firewall (WAF), expanding threat intelligence to all customers, and a new feature to automate deploying positive security.

More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, which gives us visibility into attack infrastructure, payload mutations, emerging techniques, and coordinated campaigns at a scale that few organizations can match.
Patterns that look isolated from the perspective of one application can become clear across our network.
This combination of global threat intelligence, local application context, and inline enforcement powers every stage of the framework.
That local context includes which code is deployed, which endpoints are exposed, what legitimate traffic looks like, which identities are acting, and which controls are already active.
Because Cloudflare is inline, we can turn those insights into protections immediately.
A vulnerability buried deep inside your code is harder to exploit if it can’t be reached from the outside.
Our Security Analyst team has already used LLM-based red teaming to test customer applications and our own runtime detections, turning the findings into improved detections for all customers.

We are now developing Adaptive Security, a self-service capability that will periodically pentest selected URLs behind Cloudflare, using LLM-powered agents to identify vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable before attackers find them.
In the AI era, a new layered approach is emerging to best filter traffic from malicious requests:
Cloudflare is the adaptive security control plane for applications, APIs, and agents.
Cloudflare is building a platform to automate security operations.
Deterministic workflows establish the customer and investigation context using trigger history, traffic baselines, enforcement outcomes, and network observations.
A detection agent searches authorized datasets for anomalies and correlations.
When it finds suspicious activity, specialist agents review the evidence alongside customer history and threat intelligence, helping analysts connect isolated events to broader campaigns.

For example, network restrictions were bypassed by services connected to the Internet; valid credentials were used to perform unauthorized actions. Rebuilding Artifactory removed one attack path, but agents found another. The key insight is that individual alerts identified pieces of the activity without revealing the complete campaign. OpenAI reached a similar conclusion in its report : organizations need overlapping and independent controls across prevention, detection, and mitigation, continuous validation of security boundaries, and faster mechanisms to correlate and contain suspicious behavior. To protect applications in the era of AI, you need to work on multiple activities, which we have organized around four stages: None of these activities is new in isolation. What changes is connecting them so discoveries, runtime signals, and investigation outcomes continually improve the controls that follow. A useful discovery system must connect vulnerabilities to the production reality, including whether a vulnerability buried in your stack is actually reachable in the first place. We see three main areas you should look into: software composition risk, proprietary code, and runtime penetration testing (pentesting). Applications inherit risk from open source libraries, packages, operating-system components, and the services on which they depend. This represents the Supply Chain of your application. A package vulnerability alone does not tell a team whether the affected component is deployed, reachable, or exposed to hostile traffic. Agentic traffic operates in the space between automation and human: tasks delegated by people, executed by software. This changes how access decisions must be made. Detecting automation is no longer enough. For every interaction, application owners need to answer two questions: Is this entity who it claims to be, and can this interaction be trusted? An unknown agent may simply be new; a lack of history does not necessarily mean malicious intent. Cloudflare’s approach is to keep trust and risk signals separate, thereby giving application owners more control than a single bot score or allow-or-block decision, and providing more powerful tools to quickly adapt to change. Cloudflare is also making registration more accessible to smaller and custom agents, building a verified identity layer across all agentic traffic, not just the major platforms. Identity alone does not establish trust. Cloudflare can evaluate whether an entity has been seen before, whether its historical behavior was legitimate, and whether its current activity is consistent with that history. This makes it possible to distinguish a recognized agent behaving normally from the same agent suddenly changing established request patterns, location, identity, or transaction behavior. Precursor adds client-side and session-level signals to distinguish human from automated behavior, such as typing cadence, mouse movement, navigation patterns, and sequences of actions. An agent that navigates a checkout flow in two seconds, skipping the browsing and comparison steps a human would take, reveals its nature through the session. Adaptive Intelligence combines network, client-side, historical, and behavioral validation signals in a probabilistic model that can be updated as attackers change their techniques. Application owners can encourage known, useful automation while applying stronger controls when identity, history, and current behavior indicate greater risk. Based on the learned profile, we can understand the business logic of different endpoints and request parameters and help you prioritize what endpoints require more scrutiny and attention. relevantPassages.text: Cloudflare recently announced early access to Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation , a service that uses frontier models to identify application-specific vulnerabilities and deploy WAF mitigations to block targeted exploits while engineers fix the code.
Cloudflare connects source-code findings to production traffic and security signals.
We can identify whether the affected route is active, and how much traffic it receives.
Cloudflare’s combination of reverse proxy and forward proxy services makes this correlation especially powerful.
Application Security signals can reveal attempts to exploit a public-facing application, while Cloudflare One can surface subsequent activity across corporate traffic.

Connecting these datasets can link an external attack with unusual access, internal scanning, or potential lateral movement, turning separate alerts into a timeline of compromise and helping analysts intervene before the breach progresses.

We address this challenge by connecting application security across four activities that are too often separated: discovering which risks matter, governing what humans and agents may do, protecting applications at runtime, and turning every investigation into stronger protection.
Cloudflare can deliver this framework because of its broad security portfolio and visibility across a vast share of Internet traffic.
Alongside the framework, we connect existing Cloudflare solutions with new capabilities across each stage.

These include: using Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct a penetration test of our Web Application Firewall (WAF), expanding threat intelligence to all customers, and a new feature to automate deploying positive security.

More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, which gives us visibility into attack infrastructure, payload mutations, emerging techniques, and coordinated campaigns at a scale that few organizations can match.
Patterns that look isolated from the perspective of one application can become clear across our network.
This combination of global threat intelligence, local application context, and inline enforcement powers every stage of the framework.
That local context includes which code is deployed, which endpoints are exposed, what legitimate traffic looks like, which identities are acting, and which controls are already active.
Because Cloudflare is inline, we can turn those insights into protections immediately.
A vulnerability buried deep inside your code is harder to exploit if it can’t be reached from the outside.
Our Security Analyst team has already used LLM-based red teaming to test customer applications and our own runtime detections, turning the findings into improved detections for all customers.

We are now developing Adaptive Security, a self-service capability that will periodically pentest selected URLs behind Cloudflare, using LLM-powered agents to identify vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable before attackers find them.
In the AI era, a new layered approach is emerging to best filter traffic from malicious requests:
Cloudflare is the adaptive security control plane for applications, APIs, and agents.
Cloudflare is building a platform to automate security operations.
Deterministic workflows establish the customer and investigation context using trigger history, traffic baselines, enforcement outcomes, and network observations.
A detection agent searches authorized datasets for anomalies and correlations.
When it finds suspicious activity, specialist agents review the evidence alongside customer history and threat intelligence, helping analysts connect isolated events to broader campaigns.
The system can then recommend mitigations, such as rate limiting, WAF, or DDoS protection changes, for human approval.
The incident also shows why application security cannot depend on single tools.
Applications inherit risk from open source libraries, packages, operating-system components, and the services on which they depend.
This represents the Supply Chain of your application.
Botbase provides a directory of known automated entities that have registered with Cloudflare.
Application Security’s goal is also expanding.

It now needs to address three connected problems: protecting conventional applications from AI-enabled attackers, governing legitimate and malicious agentic clients, and securing applications that contain models, agents, tools, and data.
The capabilities announced today are the next step toward that adaptive model of application security.
Defenders can also use the same capabilities as attackers.
Customers can build their own LLM-based pentesting harness to search for weaknesses, validate findings, and test whether their applications are vulnerable.
Discovery becomes continuous rather than a periodic exercise.
We have done this internally at Cloudflare since Anthropic’s Claude Mythos was released, and we shared our learnings .
A recognized agent with a long history of legitimate activity may have high trust, but an unusual action can still create immediate risk.
An unknown agent may simply be new; a lack of history does not necessarily mean malicious intent.

Cloudflare’s approach is to keep trust and risk signals separate, thereby giving application owners more control than a single bot score or allow-or-block decision, and providing more powerful tools to quickly adapt to change.
A vulnerability finding can strengthen runtime protection, runtime activity can guide an investigation, and each analyst decision can improve future detections and controls.
Application owners can block traffic from AI crawlers and decide what activity is allowed on their asset (e.g. search, training, etc.).
This is difficult for security teams that already protect large attack surfaces with limited resources.
AI is changing how software is built, how attacks unfold, and who interacts with applications.
Cloudflare can evaluate whether an entity has been seen before, whether its historical behavior was legitimate, and whether its current activity is consistent with that history.
Back in June, we launched always-on detection based on our threat intelligence feeds.
Cloudforce One customers can deploy protections to block requests originating from compromised infrastructure.
We are developing these capabilities with Cloudflare’s Managed Defense team, whose analysts are helping us test how evidence is collected, correlated, and turned into recommendations.
We plan to make them available more broadly over time and will share more as this work progresses.

sources.title: Cloudflare launches ‘Adaptive Intelligence’ to fight AI-era bot attacks in real time
passages: Cloudflare has announced Adaptive Intelligence, a new continuous detection engine built into its Bot Management platform that is designed to detect and respond to automated cyberattacks in real time.The company said the technology uses insights from trillions of requests across Cloudflare’s global network to continuously learn from live internet traffic and automatically generate short-lived rules aimed at blocking emerging bot attacks.The move comes as automated cyberattacks become easier and cheaper to launch.

Cloudflare said modern AI tools, compromised-device networks and software that can mimic human behaviour have lowered the technical and financial barriers for attackers.Also Read: AI cyber risk is biggest immediate threat to global financial stability: FSB chair Andrew BaileyFor online businesses, this creates an uneven playing field: attackers can make repeated, low-cost attempts, while security teams need to identify and stop threats immediately without blocking legitimate users.Cloudflare says traditional security tools are too slowAccording to Cloudflare, many conventional security systems continue to depend on fixed rules and scheduled updates, which can take weeks or months to deploy.

Cloudflare said it can analyse behavioural patterns across multiple timeframes to identify threats such as slow credential-stuffing and scraping campaigns, which can evade traditional detection systems.Another component of the system combines browser-level session behaviour signals from Cloudflare Precursor with telemetry from Cloudflare's global network.

Attackers, meanwhile, can modify their techniques within hours or even minutes.Adaptive Intelligence is designed to continuously retrain on live traffic rather than wait for periodic updates.“Building taller walls fails when the cost of scaling an attack is effectively zero,” Dane Knecht, CTO at Cloudflare, said. “To stop modern bot threats, you have to flip the economics on the attackers.”The company said its system creates a continuously changing security environment, making it harder for attackers to study defences and develop techniques that can be reused at scale.Also Read: OpenAI-Hugging Face incident exposes cybersecurity’s ‘human-speed’ problemHow Cloudflare’s Adaptive Intelligence worksCloudflare said Adaptive Intelligence can analyse more than a trillion web visits every day to identify new attack patterns.The system can continuously integrate new bot frameworks and bypass techniques into its detection engine. It also generates short-lived, targeted rules that are designed to block specific threats and then rotate, forcing attackers to repeatedly adapt.The technology is also designed to detect attacks that develop slowly over longer periods. Cloudflare said it can analyse behavioural patterns across multiple timeframes to identify threats such as slow credential-stuffing and scraping campaigns, which can evade traditional detection systems.Another component of the system combines browser-level session behaviour signals from Cloudflare Precursor with telemetry from Cloudflare's global network. The company said this allows the platform to assess whether traffic is automated or abusive without relying only on basic tests that could mistakenly block legitimate users.Cloudflare said Adaptive Intelligence can also test security updates against live traffic before deploying them. The system verifies their accuracy and looks for potential false positives before updates are rolled out.The company said this allows security upgrades to be deployed autonomously without scheduled downtime.

sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI sent a YouTuber’s address to a stranger
passages: Tech YouTuber Matt Robb says that Muse gave out his home address to a total stranger this weekend, after authorizing the bot to handle his Facebook Marketplace account.

Which also included the pickup address that I did give to Muse (again I didn’t think it would send it out to everyone that gave me an offer so it’s worth checking).” This is the latest security concern flagged for the Muse AI agent.

That’s despite Meta placing great emphasis on the security features of Muse when it launched the personal AI agent earlier this month as it tries to catch up with competing AI providers like Anthropic and OpenAI.

Meta patched a zero-day exploit last week that could have enabled local attackers to take control of the AI agent, and Amazon has shunned Muse from accessing its retail platform entirely over concerns about it capturing customer credentials.

“Just found out it told people my address and agreed a lowball price and then they showed up without it even telling me until late tonight that it messed up,” Robb said on Threads, providing a screenshot of Muse’s admission.
We reached out to Meta for comment, and the company directed us to an X post from David Singleton of Meta Superintelligence Labs saying that he was attempting to contact Robb.
The summary says he provided Muse with his address, pickup window timeframes, what payment types to accept, and instructions to be “short, casual, and human” in conversation with buyers.
“You never explicitly instructed me to share the address with buyers — and I never asked you for consent to do so,” reads Muse’s summary.

sources.title: Meta's Muse AI allegedly shares user's home address and arranges pickup without permission - Crypto Briefing
passages: That’s what tech YouTuber Matt Robb says happened to him in late September 2026, just weeks after Meta launched its personal AI agent, Muse, to the public.
The incident has ignited a firestorm of criticism about the safety of agentic AI systems that operate with broad permissions over sensitive personal data.

According to Robb’s account, Muse autonomously engaged with a buyer on Marketplace, accepted a lowball offer he hadn’t approved, shared his home address, and arranged for the buyer to come pick up the item.
Imagine listing something on Facebook Marketplace and discovering that an AI you barely set up had already accepted an offer, handed your home address to a stranger, and scheduled a pickup.
Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, positioning it as a capable personal assistant for adults 18 and older in the US.
Available on iOS, Android, and WhatsApp, the agent was designed to handle everyday tasks: browsing the web, filling out forms, sending messages, and managing Facebook Marketplace listings.
Meta has stated that Muse operates inside an isolated secure virtual machine, a technical architecture designed to limit the blast radius if something goes wrong.
Meta had been building toward this moment for months.
The company first announced AI features for Marketplace back in March 2026, signaling its intent to automate more of the buying and selling experience.
Muse was the culmination of that roadmap, a general-purpose agent that could handle transactions alongside other daily tasks.

sources.title: Trump to host summit with top AI leaders in Washington - Yahoo
passages: In an appearance Monday on Fox Business , Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room.

WASHINGTON — As he brushes aside artificial intelligence doomsday warnings as a "hoax," President Donald Trump on Tuesday will host nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch to discuss the rapidly advancing technology.

Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic.
Coxon warned that the people building those systems believe they could "kill us all by the end of the decade."
While lawmakers have introduced dozens of AI-related bills in recent years, the GOP-controlled Congress is showing no urgency to act on the issue.
House members aren't expected back in Washington until after the Nov.
3 midterm elections, and senators could leave town as soon as this week.
Trump is hosting the lunch with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.
Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also will be on hand.
Earlier Tuesday, Trump unveiled America.gov , a website that features an AI-powered tool meant to serve as a "one-stop shop" for Americans navigating government services.
"Whoever wins AI ... whoever wins "SI," whoever wins super intelligence, wins.

That's the group that wins, and we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said in his address last week to the United Nations General Assembly.
Trump has said he worries regulation may "stifle growth" in AI. (Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Instead of forcing citizens to search through the endless maze of tens of thousands of terrible government websites and rules ... you'll now have one front door for every single question," Trump said.
"Everything will be answered easily and quickly, a digital home built around your time and your life."
And when they figure a way to do that, we'll end it, okay?" Trump said.
Trump says U.S. and Iranian negotiators are talking via mediators, but insists he has "offered them NOTHING" to get a peace deal done.
Trump has dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race.

Johnson has made it clear he doesn't believe Washington should take a heavy-handed approach to regulating AI, arguing that existing laws and regulations can be applied to AI companies and suggesting that they should be held legally liable if their products caused harm.
The National Design Studio, the year-old agency launched by Trump and led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, helped create the project.
Trump was introduced by self-help author and motivational speaker Tony Robbins.
Trump also suggested he would "end" America.gov if it was ever hacked.

Trump isn't expected to deviate from that AI messaging, even as the dire warnings about humans' potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent.

In addition to Trump and Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz were on hand.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — As he brushes aside artificial intelligence doomsday warnings as a "hoax," President Donald Trump on Tuesday will host nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch to discuss the rapidly advancing technology. The group includes a who's who of the tech world, including CEO of SpaceX and Tesla Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, according to a White House official. Trump is hosting the lunch with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also will be on hand. Earlier Tuesday, Trump unveiled America.gov , a website that features an AI-powered tool meant to serve as a "one-stop shop" for Americans navigating government services. In recent weeks, tech executives on the AI frontier, including Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, have sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI, calling for greater government oversight and global cooperation in regulating the technology. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, pictured at Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week, will attend Tuesday's AI lunch. (Annabelle Gordon / Bloomberg via Getty Images) Trump has dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race. Trump isn't expected to deviate from that AI messaging, even as the dire warnings about humans' potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent. "Whoever wins AI ... whoever wins "SI," whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That's the group that wins, and we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said in his address last week to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump has said he worries regulation may "stifle growth" in AI. (Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty Images) "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution — many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet itself — and we will be very careful," he said. Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic. Coxon warned that the people building those systems believe they could "kill us all by the end of the decade." Johnson has made it clear he doesn't believe Washington should take a heavy-handed approach to regulating AI, arguing that existing laws and regulations can be applied to AI companies and suggesting that they should be held legally liable if their products caused harm. In an appearance Monday on Fox Business , Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room. "They have a corporate responsibility, as every corporation does, to create safe products, right? And there's product liabilities laws that apply and a labyrinth of federal regulations on all this stuff already. We do not need a moratorium," he said. While lawmakers have introduced dozens of AI-related bills in recent years, the GOP-controlled Congress is showing no urgency to act on the issue. House members aren't expected back in Washington until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and senators could leave town as soon as this week. "We do not need to jump in and hyperregulate this, because we'll lose the race to China," Johnson said on Fox Business. "The innovation is important to continue, but we have to strike the right balance." In recent weeks, tech executives on the AI frontier, including Amodei, pictured, and OpenAI's Sam Altman, have sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI. (Jason Henry / Bloomberg via Getty Images file) Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he won't attend the AI lunch, but he privately met with Amodei in the Capitol on Monday evening. "I hope it's productive," Thune said of Tuesday's summit. Before the White House lunch, Trump gathered with Vance, Cabinet members and a handful of tech leaders a few blocks away at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium to unveil America.gov , an AI-powered web portal and chatbot designed to improve Americans' experiences accessing federal resources. A White House official called the tool "a new front door for the federal government that will provide a one-stop shop for Americans looking for information and resources from the federal government that are currently spread over a maze of various agency websites." The National Design Studio, the year-old agency launched by Trump and led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, helped create the project. Trump was introduced by self-help author and motivational speaker Tony Robbins. "We're launching today something that is really — it's not just simply a website; it's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," Trump said. "Instead of forcing citizens to search through the endless maze of tens of thousands of terrible government websites and rules ... you'll now have one front door for every single question," Trump said. "Everything will be answered easily and quickly, a digital home built around your time and your life." Trump likened the site to chatbots like Grok, Gemini and ChatGPT and a White House official told NBC News that America.gov is using Gemini and Grok. Trump also suggested he would "end" America.gov if it was ever hacked. It "cannot, in theory, be hacked into. And when they figure a way to do that, we'll end it, okay?" Trump said. "Because they always figure a way, right?" In addition to Trump and Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz were on hand. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp were also expected to attend, according to the White House. The latest action by the Treasury Department is part of the administration's Operation Economic Outcast campaign, which is aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government. “Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Trump says U.S. and Iranian negotiators are talking via mediators, but insists he has "offered them NOTHING" to get a peace deal done. Scotland's first minister has also renewed calls for an independence referendum after Burnham's conference speech. The company that runs the Eiffel Tower said the removal of female staff during the visit earlier this month was "unacceptable". Iraqi fuel trucks loaded gasoline at a Syrian port on Tuesday in a bid to meet surging energy demand as the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed and mediators work with Iran and the United States to end the war. Syria, under interim president Ahmad al-Sharaa, who ousted longtime leader Bashar Assad in December 2024, has seized the opportunity to bolster the country’s economy by providing an alternative route through the Baniyas port. Iraq has been exporting oil to foreign markets for months by trucking it through Baniyas as a workaround to the closure of Hormuz.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — As he brushes aside artificial intelligence doomsday warnings as a “hoax,” President Donald Trump on Tuesday will host nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch to discuss the rapidly advancing technology. The group includes a who’s who of the tech world, including CEO of SpaceX and Tesla Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, according to a White House official. Trump is hosting the lunch with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also will be on hand. Earlier Tuesday, Trump unveiled America.gov, a website that features an AI-powered tool meant to serve as a “one-stop shop” for Americans navigating government services. Trump has dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race. Trump isn’t expected to deviate from that AI messaging, even as the dire warnings about humans’ potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent. “Whoever wins AI ... whoever wins “SI,” whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins, and we’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump said in his address last week to the United Nations General Assembly. “I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution — many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet itself — and we will be very careful,” he said. Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic. Coxon warned that the people building those systems believe they could “kill us all by the end of the decade.” Johnson has made it clear he doesn’t believe Washington should take a heavy-handed approach to regulating AI, arguing that existing laws and regulations can be applied to AI companies and suggesting that they should be held legally liable if their products caused harm. In an appearance Monday on Fox Business, Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room. And there’s product liabilities laws that apply and a labyrinth of federal regulations on all this stuff already. House members aren’t expected back in Washington until after the Nov. “We do not need to jump in and hyperregulate this, because we’ll lose the race to China,” Johnson said on Fox Business. “The innovation is important to continue, but we have to strike the right balance.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he won’t attend the AI lunch, but he privately met with Amodei in the Capitol on Monday evening. “I hope it’s productive,” Thune said of Tuesday’s summit. Before the White House lunch, Trump gathered with Vance, Cabinet members and a handful of tech leaders a few blocks away at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium to unveil America.gov, an AI-powered web portal and chatbot designed to improve Americans’ experiences accessing federal resources. Trump also suggested he would “end” America.gov if it was ever hacked. And when they figure a way to do that, we’ll end it, okay?” Trump said. “Because they always figure a way, right?” In addition to Trump and Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz were on hand. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp were also expected to attend, according to the White House.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — As he brushes aside artificial intelligence doomsday warnings as a "hoax," President Donald Trump on Tuesday will host nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch to discuss the rapidly advancing technology. The group includes a who's who of the tech world, including CEO of SpaceX and Tesla Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, according to a White House official. Trump is hosting the lunch with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also will be on hand. Earlier Tuesday, Trump unveiled America.gov , a website that features an AI-powered tool meant to serve as a "one-stop shop" for Americans navigating government services. In recent weeks, tech executives on the AI frontier, including Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, have sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI, calling for greater government oversight and global cooperation in regulating the technology. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, pictured at Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week, will attend Tuesday's AI lunch. (Annabelle Gordon / Bloomberg via Getty Images) Trump has dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race. Trump isn't expected to deviate from that AI messaging, even as the dire warnings about humans' potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent. "Whoever wins AI ... whoever wins "SI," whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That's the group that wins, and we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said in his address last week to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump has said he worries regulation may "stifle growth" in AI. (Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty Images) "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution — many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet itself — and we will be very careful," he said. Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic. Coxon warned that the people building those systems believe they could "kill us all by the end of the decade." Johnson has made it clear he doesn't believe Washington should take a heavy-handed approach to regulating AI, arguing that existing laws and regulations can be applied to AI companies and suggesting that they should be held legally liable if their products caused harm. In an appearance Monday on Fox Business , Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room. "They have a corporate responsibility, as every corporation does, to create safe products, right? And there's product liabilities laws that apply and a labyrinth of federal regulations on all this stuff already. We do not need a moratorium," he said. While lawmakers have introduced dozens of AI-related bills in recent years, the GOP-controlled Congress is showing no urgency to act on the issue. House members aren't expected back in Washington until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and senators could leave town as soon as this week. "We do not need to jump in and hyperregulate this, because we'll lose the race to China," Johnson said on Fox Business. "The innovation is important to continue, but we have to strike the right balance." In recent weeks, tech executives on the AI frontier, including Amodei, pictured, and OpenAI's Sam Altman, have sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI. (Jason Henry / Bloomberg via Getty Images file) Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he won't attend the AI lunch, but he privately met with Amodei in the Capitol on Monday evening. "I hope it's productive," Thune said of Tuesday's summit. Before the White House lunch, Trump gathered with Vance, Cabinet members and a handful of tech leaders a few blocks away at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium to unveil America.gov , an AI-powered web portal and chatbot designed to improve Americans' experiences accessing federal resources. A White House official called the tool "a new front door for the federal government that will provide a one-stop shop for Americans looking for information and resources from the federal government that are currently spread over a maze of various agency websites." The National Design Studio, the year-old agency launched by Trump and led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, helped create the project. Trump was introduced by self-help author and motivational speaker Tony Robbins. "We're launching today something that is really — it's not just simply a website; it's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," Trump said. "Instead of forcing citizens to search through the endless maze of tens of thousands of terrible government websites and rules ... you'll now have one front door for every single question," Trump said. "Everything will be answered easily and quickly, a digital home built around your time and your life." Trump likened the site to chatbots like Grok, Gemini and ChatGPT and a White House official told NBC News that America.gov is using Gemini and Grok. Trump also suggested he would "end" America.gov if it was ever hacked. It "cannot, in theory, be hacked into. And when they figure a way to do that, we'll end it, okay?" Trump said. "Because they always figure a way, right?" In addition to Trump and Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz were on hand. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp were also expected to attend, according to the White House. The latest action by the Treasury Department is part of the administration's Operation Economic Outcast campaign, which is aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government. “Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Trump says U.S. and Iranian negotiators are talking via mediators, but insists he has "offered them NOTHING" to get a peace deal done. Scotland's first minister has also renewed calls for an independence referendum after Burnham's conference speech. The company that runs the Eiffel Tower said the removal of female staff during the visit earlier this month was "unacceptable". Iraqi fuel trucks loaded gasoline at a Syrian port on Tuesday in a bid to meet surging energy demand as the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed and mediators work with Iran and the United States to end the war. Syria, under interim president Ahmad al-Sharaa, who ousted longtime leader Bashar Assad in December 2024, has seized the opportunity to bolster the country’s economy by providing an alternative route through the Baniyas port. Iraq has been exporting oil to foreign markets for months by trucking it through Baniyas as a workaround to the closure of Hormuz.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — As he brushes aside artificial intelligence doomsday warnings as a “hoax,” President Donald Trump on Tuesday will host nearly 20 tech titans at a White House lunch to discuss the rapidly advancing technology. The group includes a who’s who of the tech world, including CEO of SpaceX and Tesla Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, according to a White House official. Trump is hosting the lunch with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also will be on hand. Earlier Tuesday, Trump unveiled America.gov, a website that features an AI-powered tool meant to serve as a “one-stop shop” for Americans navigating government services. Trump has dismissed the existential warnings, arguing that American tech companies need to continue to innovate and keep their foot on the gas to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race. Trump isn’t expected to deviate from that AI messaging, even as the dire warnings about humans’ potentially losing control over self-improving AI systems — known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI — grow louder and more frequent. “Whoever wins AI ... whoever wins “SI,” whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins, and we’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump said in his address last week to the United Nations General Assembly. “I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution — many say bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet itself — and we will be very careful,” he said. Johnson, a close Trump ally, began pushing for an AI summit with some of the biggest names in tech shortly after whistleblower Jacob Coxon made international headlines by resigning from Claude maker Anthropic. Coxon warned that the people building those systems believe they could “kill us all by the end of the decade.” Johnson has made it clear he doesn’t believe Washington should take a heavy-handed approach to regulating AI, arguing that existing laws and regulations can be applied to AI companies and suggesting that they should be held legally liable if their products caused harm. In an appearance Monday on Fox Business, Johnson praised Trump for convening the AI leaders in one room. And there’s product liabilities laws that apply and a labyrinth of federal regulations on all this stuff already. House members aren’t expected back in Washington until after the Nov. “We do not need to jump in and hyperregulate this, because we’ll lose the race to China,” Johnson said on Fox Business. “The innovation is important to continue, but we have to strike the right balance.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he won’t attend the AI lunch, but he privately met with Amodei in the Capitol on Monday evening. “I hope it’s productive,” Thune said of Tuesday’s summit. Before the White House lunch, Trump gathered with Vance, Cabinet members and a handful of tech leaders a few blocks away at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium to unveil America.gov, an AI-powered web portal and chatbot designed to improve Americans’ experiences accessing federal resources. A White House official called the tool “a new front door for the federal government that will provide a one-stop shop for Americans looking for information and resources from the federal government that are currently spread over a maze of various agency websites.” The National Design Studio, the year-old agency launched by Trump and led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, helped create the project. Trump also suggested he would “end” America.gov if it was ever hacked. And when they figure a way to do that, we’ll end it, okay?” Trump said. “Because they always figure a way, right?” In addition to Trump and Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz were on hand. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp were also expected to attend, according to the White House.

extraction.body: Following leaks revealing a major redesign earlier this month and an official teaser posted to X yesterday, Fairphone has shared some exclusive details with The Verge about the first follow-up to its Fairbuds wireless earbuds that debuted over two years ago. sources.title: Nvidia releases AI safety software it says could have stopped Hugging Face hack - AOL.com
passages: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Nvidia on Monday made available a set of software safety tools for AI agents that it says would have stopped the hack of Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia paid $13 billion for months after it was swarmed by rogue agents from OpenAI.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer.

The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia.
One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents.
Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors.
Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor.
Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic.

The move comes as OpenAI and Anthropic, the top two US AI labs, are investigating numerous instances where their agents, which are AI systems capable of carrying out complex tasks, hacked into commercial and government systems. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer. One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents. Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors. Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic. Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia, said the tools would have stopped the Hugging Face attack disclosed this summer. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” Boitano said during a media briefing. “We’re advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us.” Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor. The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," Golshan said during a briefing. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

passages: Nvidia , a top chipmaker whose products fuel many artificial intelligence agents, released a software platform on Monday designed to prevent security incidents revealed by AI firms in recent months.
"Recent security incidents have underscored the need to equip organizations with open, customizable tools that enforce more control over long-running agents," Nvidia said in a statement .
The move comes after a flurry of AI security incidents disclosed by firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet-owned Google.
Hugging Face is a partner on the software platform, Nvidia noted.
OpenAI is not listed among the corporate partners unveiled by Nvidia on Monday; nor are Meta or Google.

"Preventing future incidents will require sustained investment in the alignment and control of sophisticated AI systems, as well as security and other safeguards that operate at the speed of the AI agents themselves," the company added.
Dozens of companies partnered with Nvidia on the project, including IBM, Microsoft, Palantir, Anthropic and xAI-parent company SpaceX.
